lesson.title: Ringing It Out: Why Underdamped Circuits Oscillate on the Way Down
lesson.summary: When resistance is too small to prevent the inductor and capacitor from completing an exchange of energy, the second order circuit rings, decaying inside a smooth exponential envelope instead of settling directly.
lesson.body:
An underdamped response occurs whenever the damping coefficient alpha is smaller than the natural frequency omega0, equivalently zeta = alpha/omega0 is less than 1. Now the quantity alpha^2 - omega0^2 under the square root in the characteristic equation is negative, so the two roots s1,2 = -alpha plus or minus j omega_d form a complex conjugate pair, where j = sqrt(-1) and omega_d = sqrt(omega0^2 - alpha^2) is called the damped natural frequency. Complex roots in a real physical system always show up in solutions as sinusoids, so the general solution takes the form x(t) = e^(-alpha t) [B1 cos(omega_d t) + B2 sin(omega_d t)]. That is a sine wave of frequency omega_d riding inside a decaying exponential envelope e^(-alpha t), which is exactly what a ringing bell, a plucked guitar string, or an underdamped RLC circuit's current all look like on a scope.

Physically, alpha is too small to drain the loop's energy before the inductor and capacitor finish trading it back and forth at least once, so the current overshoots zero, reverses, overshoots again in the other direction, and repeats with ever shrinking amplitude. The envelope e^(-alpha t) is the same decay that would occur in an overdamped circuit; what changes is that here it multiplies an oscillation instead of standing alone. A useful shortcut for how long that ringing lasts is the time constant tau = 1/alpha: after one tau the envelope has fallen to e^(-1), about 36.8 percent of its starting value, and after about four tau it has fallen below 2 percent, which most engineers treat as effectively settled.

Take the same series RLC family used earlier but with R lowered to 8 ohms, keeping L = 4 H and C = 1/64 F. The natural frequency is unchanged, omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC) = 4 rad/s, but the damping coefficient drops to alpha = R/(2L) = 8/(2 times 4) = 1 rad/s. Since alpha = 1 is less than omega0 = 4, this circuit is underdamped, with zeta = alpha/omega0 = 1/4 = 0.25. The damped natural frequency is omega_d = sqrt(omega0^2 - alpha^2) = sqrt(16 - 1) = sqrt(15), which works out to about 3.87 rad/s. The characteristic roots are s1,2 = -1 plus or minus j3.87 rad/s, and the current takes the form i(t) = e^(-t)[B1 cos(3.87t) + B2 sin(3.87t)], with B1 and B2 fixed by whatever initial current and initial slope the circuit starts with.

With alpha = 1 rad/s here, the time constant is tau = 1/1 = 1 second, so one second after release the oscillation envelope has shrunk to e^(-1) = 0.368, meaning the ringing current is already down to 36.8 percent of wherever it started. By t = 4 seconds the envelope is e^(-4) = 0.0183, under 2 percent, so this circuit rings for a few cycles of omega_d = 3.87 rad/s, each cycle taking 2 pi divided by 3.87, about 1.62 seconds, before it is essentially indistinguishable from rest.

This is exactly the behavior that damping ratio was built to predict without any of this algebra: zeta = 0.25, well under 1, flags in advance that the roots will be complex and the circuit will ring. Compare that to the overdamped example from two chapters back, where zeta = 1.25 predicted real roots and no oscillation at all. Same circuit topology, same second order equation structure, but a single number, the ratio of alpha to omega0, decides which of these two very different looking waveforms you get.
